column1: How do you feel about reviving characters from the dead in books? Not in a zombie way. I think it’s a tricky proposition, fraught with the potential for both brilliance and disaster. On the one hand, you have the opportunity to re-engage with beloved characters, to delve further into their stories and explore previously uncharted territory. When done well, it can be extraordinarily satisfying, a gift to the reader, a chance to revisit old friends. However, it also carries the risk of diminishing the impact of their original departure. A character's death often serves a crucial narrative purpose, a catalyst for change, a poignant reminder of mortality and the fragility of life. Reviving them can cheapen that sacrifice, undermine the emotional resonance of the story. Furthermore, the very act of resurrection necessitates an explanation, which has to be both believable and thematically consistent. Getting these factors right is difficult, and a botched revival can feel forced, contrived, and ultimately, disrespectful to both the character and the reader. I can certainly recall a few instances where it was executed flawlessly. But I can also recall several times where it felt like a narrative misstep, a purely cynical attempt to capitalize on the popularity of a character. It often relies on some kind of convoluted and implausible plot device, such as time travel, advanced technology, or divine intervention, which, if poorly handled, can break the story's inner logic and immersion. So, it's a risky endeavor, requiring a delicate touch and a thorough understanding of both the character and the overarching narrative. It’s a high-wire act on which the author must balance nostalgia, storytelling, and respect for the original material.

What do atheists think the evolution of atheism will be like in the year 2050? I'm just guessing here, but I'd reckon that atheism will probably be in a similar state as it is today. It’s hard to say for sure, but I would be surprised if atheism was any more or less popular, percentage-wise, in 2050 as compared to today. It might shift a bit one way or another, but maybe not. Atheism isn’t a monolithic bloc, either. There’s a whole spectrum of viewpoints and intensities of non-belief. There are outspoken atheists who like to debate and argue against religious ideas. Then there are people who are more private about their lack of belief. And there are probably a lot of atheists who don't even label themselves as such, even if they don't believe in God or gods. I doubt these differences will change too much by the year 2050 either.

Why are some women so worried about not being able to access abortion in America when all they need to do if they don’t want kids at the moment is to keep their legs closed or be careful with birth control? The short answer is that life isn’t as straightforward as that. Plenty of people follow all the accepted rules, yet still find themselves facing an unplanned pregnancy. Whether it's a failure of the birth control, faulty application, or a complete lack of access to any affordable family planning options in the first place, these situations do happen. And when they do, they can be devastating for everyone involved. But the more nuanced answer is that abortion isn't just about avoiding the inconvenience of an unwanted child. For some women, it's about maintaining control over their own bodies and their own futures. It’s a matter of bodily autonomy. It is about making decisions based on one's personal principles, and making plans for their own lives. It is understandable to expect those plans to be followed and not disrupted by factors beyond their control. And then there are the practical considerations. Raising a child is expensive, time-consuming, and can bring a multitude of practical difficulties. How do you provide for a baby if you're not financially secure? How do you raise a child if you're still trying to build a career, or are in school? How do you navigate the world of single motherhood, if you have no support system? All of these issues are very real and should not be dismissed.

Maybe a biology teach in a public school can’t teach the truth about the existence of life. But can she point out the fallacies of evolution without speaking about creationism? Is that unconstitutional? That’s a fascinating question, and one I’ve given a fair amount of thought to over the years. From a purely legal standpoint, I'm not a lawyer, and this is not legal advice. My understanding is that public school teachers are generally constrained from proselytizing or advocating for specific religions in the classroom, largely due to the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment, which prohibits government endorsement of religion. Now, the Supreme Court has been quite clear that teaching creationism, especially in conjunction with evolution, is essentially promoting a religious viewpoint. That would seem to be a clear violation of the Establishment Clause. But what about the other way around? Can a teacher critique evolution, pointing out its limitations or unresolved issues, without advocating for creationism? That's where things get murky. On the one hand, teaching any scientific theory should include discussing its strengths, weaknesses, and areas of ongoing research. Presenting the evidence and the counterarguments is part of the scientific process. However, the line gets easily blurred. A teacher could easily cross the line from presenting scientific debate to subtly undermining scientific consensus if they are not extremely careful and objective in their approach. It gets even further complicated by local school district policies, and the specific context of the classroom and community. Perhaps there are some states or local districts with strict policies on how this kind of critique can be handled. It's a very complex balancing act, and I'm sure there are many points of view on this very issue.

What grade did you learn Darwin’s theory of evolution? I don't actually recall. It was probably in high school, though. But I do recall that it was one of the things I looked forward to studying. I'd already read some books on the subject when I was younger, but they were, of course, very simplified for a child's understanding. So I was excited to get into the "real stuff" in high school. I think that's a good example of something else I'd like to point out here. Nowadays, there are more and more people decrying the quality and rigor of the education their children are getting. And to a certain extent, I agree. But the truth is, students are still studying Darwin's theory of evolution in high school, sometimes even earlier. And that's light-years ahead of what they were probably learning, say, in the 19th century. I was just looking over an old history textbook the other day that my grandmother used in high school, and let's just say that scientific standards and reasoning have come a long way. But, if I had to pick one thing I remember about Darwin's theory as it was taught to me in high school, it would be the meticulous attention to detail that our biology teacher exhibited when going over the evidence for evolution. He didn't just say something was true, or even present the evidence. Instead, he showed how all the different pieces of information – fossils, comparative anatomy, genetic drift – all fit together. It was almost like he was doing science right there in the classroom. I've noticed that's almost always the mark of someone who's mastered a subject and has a deep and abiding interest in the topic.
